english: Ice is made of water, yet is colder than water.
Wood straight enough to meet the marking line is steamed and bent into a wheel, its curvature meeting the compass.
Though it wither and parch in the sun, it will not straighten again, because steaming and bending have made it so.
Therefore wood, marked by the line, becomes straight; metal, whetted on a stone, becomes sharp.
If the gentleman learns widely and each day examines himself repeatedly, his knowledge will grow clear and his conduct without fault.
I once pondered all day long, and it was not as good as a moment's learning.
I once stood on tiptoe to gaze afar, and it was not as good as the broad view from climbing a height.
Climbing high and beckoning, the arm is no longer, yet it can be seen from afar.
Shouting with the wind, the voice is no stronger, yet it is heard more distinctly.
He who borrows horses and carriage is not swift of foot, yet reaches a thousand li.
He who borrows boat and oars is no swimmer, yet crosses rivers.
When earth piles up into a mountain, wind and rain arise therefrom.
When water gathers into a deep pool, dragons are born therefrom.
When good deeds accumulate into virtue, spiritual insight comes of itself and the sage's mind is complete.
Therefore without accumulating half-steps, one cannot reach a thousand li;
without gathering small streams, one cannot form rivers and seas.
A fine steed in one leap cannot cover ten paces;
a nag in ten days' journey succeeds by not giving up.
Carve but give up, and even rotten wood will not break;
carve without giving up, and metal and stone can be engraved.
The crab has six legs and two pincers, yet unless it lodges in the burrow of snakes and eels it has nowhere to dwell—because its mind is restless.
Hence, without deep and quiet resolve, there is no shining clarity;
without obscure, hidden toil, there is no towering achievement.
In ancient times those who studied must have had teachers.
A teacher is one who transmits the Way, imparts learning, and dispels doubts.
Men are not born knowing everything; who can be without doubts?
If one has doubts and does not follow a teacher, those doubts remain forever unresolved.
If one born before me understood the Way before me, I follow him and take him as my teacher;
if one born after me understood the Way before me, I too follow him and take him as my teacher.
I take the Way as my teacher; why should I care whether he was born before or after me?
Hence, no matter noble or base, old or young, wherever the Way exists, there the teacher exists.
Alas, the tradition of honouring teachers has long been untransmitted!
How hard it is to expect men to be free of delusions!
The sages of antiquity, far surpassing ordinary men, still followed teachers and asked questions of them;
the common crowd of today, far below the sages, yet feel ashamed to learn from teachers.
Hence the sage grows ever more sage, the fool ever more foolish.
Is it not all from this that the sage became sage and the fool became fool?
Loving his son, a man chooses a teacher to instruct him;
but for himself he is ashamed to take a teacher—how deluded!
That teacher of a child merely teaches him the book and drills him in punctuation; he is not what I call one who transmits the Way and dispels doubts.
Ignorant of punctuation he seeks a teacher; unable to resolve his doubts he does not—learning the small while losing the great: I see no wisdom in this.
Witch-doctors, musicians and artisans feel no shame in learning from one another.
But when gentlemen of rank speak of teachers and disciples, they flock together and laugh at them.
Ask why, and they say: he and he are of similar age, and their learning alike.
To take one of low rank as teacher seems shameful; to take a high official seems near flattery.
That the tradition of teachers will not revive is clear! Witch-doctors, musicians and artisans are scorned by gentlemen, yet now the gentlemen's wisdom proves less than theirs—how strange indeed!
The sage had no fixed teacher.
Confucius took Tanzi, Changhong, Shixiang and Laodan as his teachers.
Men like Tanzi were not the equal of Confucius in worth.
Confucius said: "When three walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher."
Hence a disciple need not be inferior to his teacher, nor the teacher superior to his disciple; the order of understanding the Way differs, and each has his speciality—that is all.
Li Pan, a youth of seventeen, loves the ancient prose, and has studied all the classics and their commentaries of the Six Arts; unbound by the fashion of the times, he studies with me.
I praise him for honouring the ancient tradition, and wrote this "Discourse on Teachers" to give him.
